title: Logical Validity
body:
An argument is **valid** when the conclusion cannot be false while all the premises are true.
The definition is about structure, so a valid argument can have false premises and a false
conclusion.

```
All cats are reptiles.        false
All reptiles have scales.     false
So all cats have scales.      false

Valid: IF the premises were true, the conclusion would have to be.
```

```
All cats are mammals.         true
Felix is a mammal.            true
So Felix is a cat.            true, and the argument is INVALID
```

The second argument has true premises and a true conclusion and is broken, because Felix could
have been a dog and the premises would still hold. Validity asks whether the premises guarantee
the conclusion, and truth is a separate question answered by [[Soundness]].

Two ways to establish it. A [[Truth Table]] checks every assignment and reports validity
when no row makes the premises true and the conclusion false. [[Natural Deduction]]
derives the conclusion from the premises by rules. To establish invalidity, build a
[[Counter-Model]].
